title: Nubia's churches
hook: Christian kingdoms once flourished on the Nile in what is now Sudan, and their churches were almost forgotten

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lalibela, where churches were carved down into the rock. Your line was churches in the rock. Did you keep your carved-out hour safe? Day eight hundred forty.

Sand, blown over the ruins of a town by the Nile. Archaeologists dig, and under the sand they find walls, and on the walls, faces. Saints with large dark eyes. Angels. Mary holding her child. A bishop, painted in his robes, looking straight out at them as if he'd been waiting. These are the walls of a cathedral, in a place called Faras, in old Nubia, the land along the Nile south of Egypt. Whole Christian kingdoms once lived here. Their names had mostly faded from memory. Today: Nubia's churches.

The Bible already knows this land, though it calls it Ethiopia, its word for the country south of Egypt. A Psalm says, in the King James Bible, "Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God." And in Acts, Philip meets on the road "a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians." He's reading Isaiah, he asks to be baptized, and he goes on his way rejoicing. Some readers place his queen's kingdom in the land later called Nubia. Later, kings along the Nile became Christian, and their kingdoms, Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia, built churches and cathedrals, with bishops and monasteries, and walls covered in paintings. They worshiped in Greek and Coptic, and wrote in their own Nubian language too. For a long time they flourished. Then, slowly, the kingdoms weakened, and the churches emptied. There was no single dramatic fall, the way there was at Constantinople. The faith faded out of the valley, and sand covered the walls. And that's why this day matters. Christian history isn't only Rome, Constantinople and the cathedrals of Europe. It reached Africa early, riding home with that traveler from Philip's road, and it grew along the Nile. This week ran from Jan Hus seeking the truth, Thomas à Kempis in his nook, Joan's humble answer, the last liturgy in Hagia Sophia, Gutenberg's letters, churches in the rock at Lalibela, and now faces under the sand. To remember a church is to say: these people were here, and they prayed.

Here's the practice: learn one lost church's name. Say the kingdoms' names slowly, once each: Nobadia. Makuria. Alodia. Then the town: Faras. Picture the painted bishop on the wall, the saints with their wide eyes, the people who once stood in front of them on an ordinary morning. You don't know their names. You can hold them for a minute anyway. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, let the names be enough. The bell holds the time.
Nubia's churches. The churches of the Christian kingdoms on the Nile, in what is now Sudan, which faded and were found again under the sand.
Your line: remembered churches. Today, tell one person the name Faras, or Makuria, and what was found there. A name said aloud is a name remembered. Day eight hundred forty.

howItsDone: The Nubian churches no longer hold services, but paintings from the cathedral at Faras are kept in museums, and Christians in Sudan and elsewhere sometimes remember the Nubian kingdoms as part of their own story.

notes: Claims rule: the outline hook's 'eight hundred years' is not stated; no dates are given. Confirm.
'Some readers place his queen's kingdom in the land later called Nubia': Candace (Kandake) as the title of queens of Kush/Meroë; attributed to 'some readers'. Confirm.
Nobadia, Makuria, Alodia; worship in Greek and Coptic with Old Nubian writing; slow decline rather than a single conquest: confirm the summary.
Faras cathedral paintings (saints, angels, Mary, bishops) found under sand; now in museums (Warsaw and Khartoum). Confirm.
'It was African from the start' rests on Acts 8; confirm phrasing is fair and not an overclaim.
Week end (day 840 = week 120): the teach looks back at days 834–840.
The Ethiopian eunuch is in the KJV quotation; the script otherwise calls him an official/traveler.
